title: Identifying the signatures of residual activity in harmonically bound active Brownian dynamics
abstract: A confined self-propelled particle exhibits a range of intriguing dynamical phenomena dictated by the interplay between the intrinsic activity of the particle and the imposed confinement. This competition manifests as a crossover in the steady-state position distribution of a harmonically bound active Brownian particle (HBABP) from Boltzmann-like to bimodal, commonly recognized as the passive and active regimes, respectively, upon variations in activity and confinement strength. We present a comprehensive analysis of the resultant dynamics of an HBABP employing analytical calculations and numerical simulations, examining the variations in the position distribution, residual or resultant velocity, mean square displacement, power spectral density, and effective harmonic confinement at varying activities in the characteristic regimes across the crossover. These analyses provide a reliable identification of the signature of residual or remnant activity in ABP dynamics after being impeded by the harmonic confinement. Our results show that the resultant HBABP dynamics in the regime with a Boltzmann-like position distribution is dominated by residual activity, and the motion in the other regime, with a bimodal position distribution, is similar to that of a harmonically bound Brownian particle--devoid of residual activity--at a displaced position, where the activity is balanced by the restoring force field.
summary: The paper investigates how self-propelled particles confined by a harmonic potential behave under different activity levels. By analyzing multiple dynamical signatures—including MSD and PSD—the authors distinguish between regimes where residual activity dominates versus those where the activity is effectively quenched by the confining force field.
main_problem: The study aims to reliably identify and quantify the signature of residual or remnant activity in the dynamics of an Active Brownian Particle (ABP) confined within a harmonic potential.
main_result: The nature of the particle's motion depends critically on the ratio between the persistence time ($	au_R$) and the confinement equilibration time ($	au_k$): $	au_R \ll 	au_k$ shows residual activity signatures, while $	au_R \gg 	au_k$ suggests the activity is balanced by the restoring force.
method: The analysis combines analytical calculations of correlation functions and position distributions with numerical simulations solving the underlying Langevin equations for the system.
model_or_system: The model describes an ABP undergoing self-propulsion ($V$) confined in 2D by a harmonic potential $U(r) =  rac{1}{2}kr^2$. The dynamics are governed by coupled Langevin equations involving propulsion, confinement restoring forces, and thermal noise.
key_observables: Position distribution ($P_{ss}(r)$), residual/resultant velocity components ($\mathbf{v}_{	ext{res}}$), Mean Square Displacement (MSD), and Power Spectral Density (PSD).
important_parameters: Activity strength quantified by the Péclet number ($	ext{Pe}$); characteristic timescales $	au_R$ (persistence time) and $	au_k$ (confinement equilibration time).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on examining two extreme limits ($	au_R \ll 	au_k$ and $	au_R \gg 	au_k$) and assumes that cross-terms involving uncorrelated Brownian velocity noises vanish.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate position distributions ($P(x, t), P(y, t)$) and steady-state radial distributions $P_{ss}(r)$, comparing analytical predictions to simulations across different activity regimes.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the dynamics by deriving theoretical expressions for observables (like MSD and distribution functions) in the two limiting cases ($	au_R \ll 	au_k$ and $	au_R \gg 	au_k$), contrasting these results with the passive Brownian counterpart ($V=0$).
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, multi-diagnostic framework (beyond just distribution shape) to characterize non-equilibrium steady states in active matter systems, which is highly relevant for understanding energy dissipation and effective potentials in complex physical settings.
